- When sentiment is high (≥0.7) and forecast spikes upward, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid overreaction.  
- If sentiment drops sharply (≤0.4) after a spike, model should not overshoot downward — cap decline to avoid excessive sell-off.  
- Forecast mean should align with recent 7–14 day average of price history, not latest 30d trend.  
- Overshoots after sentiment spikes (especially >0.9) are common — apply a “cooling-off” correction: subtract 2–5% from peak forecast.  
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 75–80), model should not continue upward trend — adjust forecast downward by 3–8% for next 3–5 days.  
- Sentiment history with low variance (e.g., 0.4–0.6) should trigger conservative forecast — avoid large swings, especially if history shows volatility clustering.  
- When sentiment is low and price is trending down, forecast should not lag — adjust to match recent 5-day moving average to avoid underestimating decline.
